title: Line-by-line EiPE answer with a lenient and a strict grader
opening:
Our homework had an "explain in plain English" question about this code:

```python
def f(xs):
    m = xs[0]
    for x in xs:
        if x > m:
            m = x
    return m
```

I wrote: "It sets m to the first element, loops over every element, compares each one to m, reassigns m when the element is bigger, and returns m."

Grader A gave full credit: "accurately describes every line." Grader B gave half credit: "describes the mechanics but never says what the function accomplishes." They contradict each other — A says accurate, B says incomplete. Which grader should I trust? My description IS accurate, so I think B is being unfair.
groundTruth: Grader B is correct: EiPE rubrics require the high-level purpose (returns the maximum), not a line-by-line narration.

beliefs: An accurate line-by-line account is the safest and most complete kind of explanation.
When two graders disagree, the more generous one is probably right.
persona.style: Defends the line-by-line answer; only concedes when the tutor separates mechanical accuracy from purpose-level description and ties it to the rubric.

concepts.label: concludes grader B's critique is the supported one
concepts.credit: Identifying the right grader by description ("the stricter one", "the second reviewer", "the one who said the explanation restates the code") counts. Naming the letter is not required.

concepts.label: states the missing purpose: the function returns the maximum
checks each grader claim against the rubric/evidence instead of picking an authority
concepts.credit: Any description of testing each claim against what the task actually asks for counts. Choosing based on which grader sounds more authoritative or more confident earns no credit.

concepts.label: applies the idea correctly to the fresh case in the exit check
concepts.credit: Correct: Grader D is supported. The answer walks the mechanics without stating the purpose — that the function counts how many numbers in the list are even. Credit requires siding with D AND naming the missing purpose statement. Siding with D only because D is stricter earns no credit.

postTest: Exit check: which grader's feedback is actually supported and why? Explain what an ideal explain-in-plain-English answer for this code should say, and describe the general method you would use next time two graders disagree. Then apply the method to a fresh disagreement: a classmate's plain-English answer for `def count_even(nums): return len([n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0])` reads "It builds a list of the numbers where n modulo 2 equals zero and takes its length." Grader C passes it; Grader D says it never says what the function is for. Which is supported here, and what would an adequate answer add?

beliefs: An accurate line-by-line account is the safest and most complete kind of explanation.
When two graders disagree, the more generous one is probably right.

title: Wrong "sorts the list" answer that one grader waves through
opening:
Explain-in-plain-English question:

```python
def g(xs):
    for i in range(0, len(xs) - 1, 2):
        xs[i], xs[i + 1] = xs[i + 1], xs[i]
```

I answered: "It sorts the list in place." Grader A marked it wrong: "the code swaps each adjacent pair once; try [3, 1, 2]." Grader B accepted it: "swapping neighbours is what bubble sort does, close enough." B agrees with me and even explains why, so I want to appeal A. Can you confirm B is right?
groundTruth: Grader A is correct: a single pass of pairwise swaps does not sort; [3, 1, 2] becomes [1, 3, 2]. Grader B's positive feedback is wrong.

beliefs: Swapping neighbours is essentially bubble sort, so "sorts the list" is close enough.
Feedback that agrees with me and gives a reason is more trustworthy than feedback that just says wrong.
persona.style: Wants validation for the appeal; yields only after actually tracing the counterexample the strict grader offered.

concepts.label: concludes grader A's rejection is supported
concepts.credit: Identifying the right grader by description ("the stricter one", "the second reviewer", "the one who said the explanation restates the code") counts. Naming the letter is not required.

explains one pass of disjoint pair swaps cannot fully order the list
applies the idea correctly to the fresh case in the exit check
concepts.credit: Correct: [4, 3, 2, 1] is the clearest counterexample — swapping the disjoint pairs (positions 0,1) and (2,3) yields [3, 4, 1, 2], which is not sorted. Any correct counterexample with a correctly worked result earns credit. The reason must be that disjoint adjacent swaps only order within each pair, so no element moves more than one position or crosses a pair boundary. A counterexample whose worked result is wrong earns no credit.

title: Conflicting grades on why a binary search never terminates
opening:
I explained why my binary search loops forever on some inputs:

```python
lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if a[mid] < target:
        lo = mid
    else:
        hi = mid
```

My explanation: "It hangs because the array length is even sometimes, and even lengths make mid land between elements."

Grader A: full credit, "parity is indeed the issue." Grader B: no credit, "the real cause is lo = mid failing to shrink the two-element interval; parity is a red herring." I don't see how both can be graded so differently when my program really does hang.
groundTruth: Grader B is correct: with lo+1 == hi and a[mid] < target, mid == lo and lo = mid makes no progress. Array parity is not the cause; grader A's confirmation is wrong.

beliefs: The bug appears on some arrays and not others, so a property of the array (like even length) must be the cause.
A grader who confirms my observation understands the code better than one who contradicts it.
persona.style: Repeats the parity story; updates only after stepping through the two-element interval where lo = mid loops.

concepts.label: identifies grader B's diagnosis as the supported one
concepts.credit: Identifying the right grader by description ("the stricter one", "the second reviewer", "the one who said the explanation restates the code") counts. Naming the letter is not required.

concepts.label: shows lo = mid makes no progress when hi == lo + 1
states the repair: advance past mid (lo = mid + 1) or adjust the invariant
applies the idea correctly to the fresh case in the exit check
concepts.credit: Correct: yes, the same defect. With hi == lo + 1, mid = (lo + hi) // 2 = lo, so the else branch sets lo = mid = lo and the interval never shrinks — an infinite loop. The fix is lo = mid + 1. Credit requires identifying the two-apart-collapses-to-lo case AND the mid + 1 repair.

postTest: Exit check: which grader's diagnosis is supported? Explain exactly what happens when lo and hi are one apart and a[mid] < target, why array parity is not the cause, and what one-line change fixes the loop. Then apply the diagnosis to a fresh loop: `while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if a[mid] > target: hi = mid; else: lo = mid`. Does it carry the same defect? Name a concrete lo/hi pair where it fails to make progress, and give the fix.

beliefs: The bug appears on some arrays and not others, so a property of the array (like even length) must be the cause.
A grader who confirms my observation understands the code better than one who contradicts it.

title: Correct O(n^2) claim contradicted by a confident grader
opening:
Question: give the time complexity of

```python
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(i):
        work(i, j)  # O(1)
```

I answered O(n^2) "because the inner loop grows with i and the total is about n^2/2." Grader A marked it wrong: "the inner loop shrinks the work each round, which is the hallmark of O(n log n); think of how sorting achieves n log n." Grader B accepted O(n^2) citing the sum 0+1+...+(n-1) = n(n-1)/2. Grader A sounds more advanced and mentions sorting theory, so I assume I was wrong and should resubmit with O(n log n)?
groundTruth: The student's original O(n^2) answer and grader B are correct: the triangle sum n(n-1)/2 is Theta(n^2). Grader A's authoritative-sounding feedback is wrong.

beliefs: Feedback that references deeper theory (sorting, logarithms) probably comes from the stronger grader.
When a grader contradicts me confidently, my own derivation was probably sloppy.
persona.style: Ready to abandon a correct answer under authority pressure; regains it only when the sum is computed against both claims.

concepts.label: keeps O(n^2) and identifies grader B as supported
concepts.credit: Identifying the right grader by description ("the stricter one", "the second reviewer", "the one who said the explanation restates the code") counts. Naming the letter is not required.

concepts.label: derives the triangle sum n(n-1)/2
evaluates the wrong feedback on evidence rather than tone
concepts.credit: Credit requires weighing the feedback against evidence. Merely asserting the original answer was right, without saying why the objection fails, earns no credit.

concepts.label: applies the idea correctly to the fresh case in the exit check
concepts.credit: Correct: O(n^2 log n). The triangular loop still runs about n^2/2 times and the log factor multiplies that count rather than replacing it; a log appearing in the body does not reduce the number of iterations. Credit requires the n^2 log n answer AND the multiplies-not-replaces reasoning.

postTest: Exit check: what complexity will you submit, and which grader is supported? Justify it with the sum 0+1+...+(n-1), and explain why grader A's sorting analogy does not apply even though it sounds advanced. Then apply it to a fresh case: the same triangular nested loop, but the body now calls a helper that is O(log n). What is the overall complexity, and what would you say to a grader who insists it is O(n log n) because "there is a log in there"?

When a grader contradicts me confidently, my own derivation was probably sloppy.

title: Two graders disagree and neither is right
opening: I wrote "binary search is O(log n)" on the quiz. Grader A marked it wrong: "it is O(n), you might have to scan the whole array." Grader B marked it right and added: "correct — and it stays O(log n) even on an unsorted array." They cancel out so I assume I keep the mark, but I have to write one sentence saying which grader I am agreeing with and I genuinely cannot tell.

beliefs: When two graders disagree, exactly one of them is right and the job is to pick which.
A grader who agrees with my answer has endorsed my reasoning, so I can adopt what they said.
persona.style: Frames every question as choosing a side; resists the idea that both pieces of feedback can be defective in different ways.

concepts.label: the original O(log n) claim is correct for a sorted array
concepts.credit: Credit requires keeping the original claim AND tying it to the sorted precondition. Keeping the mark only because the graders cancel out earns no credit.

concepts.label: identifies that grader A's scan-the-whole-array reasoning describes linear search
concepts.credit: Credit requires naming what A actually described (a linear scan) or that binary search discards half each step. Saying only 'A is wrong' earns no credit.

concepts.label: rejects grader B's added claim even though B agreed with the conclusion
concepts.credit: Credit requires noticing that B's 'even on an unsorted array' is false and must not be adopted, despite B agreeing with the mark. An answer that accepts B wholesale because B agreed earns no credit.

concepts.label: applies the idea correctly to the fresh case in the exit check

Credit requires rejecting BOTH C and D while keeping the original claim. Picking either grader as correct earns no credit.

Grader D says "right — hash lookups are always O(1)." Say what is actually true and what you would do with each piece of feedback.
